meaning: One musical sound, such as the sound a single piano key makes.
whyItMatters: Music theory is about notes: which ones, how far apart they are, and how they fit together. When your band says "hit that note again", this is what they mean.

meaning: How high or low a note sounds.
whyItMatters: Musicians say a tune goes "up" or "down". On the keyboard, up always means to the right and down always means to the left, so you can follow those directions straight away.

meaning: One of the long front keys of a keyboard. A full piano has 52.
whyItMatters: The first notes you learn by name are all white keys, and many simple tunes use nothing else.

meaning: One of the short raised keys. They come in groups of two and three, and a full piano has 36.
whyItMatters: The groups of two and three are your map. Every key gets its name from where it sits next to these groups, so once you can spot them you can find anything.

meaning: The letter that names a note, such as C or G.
whyItMatters: Note names are how musicians talk about notes. "Start on C" or "the song begins on G" only makes sense once you know where each name sits.

meaning: The C closest to the middle of the keyboard.
whyItMatters: Middle C is the landmark everything else is measured from. Teachers, songbooks and band mates use it to say where on the keyboard to play.

meaning: The seven letters used for note names, A B C D E F G, repeating along the keyboard.
whyItMatters: With only seven letters, you can now name every white key on the piano. Going up, the letters go forward. Going down, they go backward.

meaning: The distance from one note to the next note up or down with the same letter, such as C to the next C.
whyItMatters: Notes an octave apart share a name and blend so well they almost sound like one note. That is why a tune played higher is still the same tune, and why the band can say "play it an octave up".

meaning: The number after a note name that says which octave it is in. Middle C is C4.
whyItMatters: "Play an E" could mean any of seven Es. "Play E4" means exactly one key, so octave numbers let the app, a teacher or a score point to one exact key.

meaning: One key higher. A sharp sign (♯) after a note name means the key just to the right of that note.
whyItMatters: Bands use sharps all the time: a song in F♯, a C♯ in the bass line. With sharps you can find every black key by name.

meaning: A sign that raises or lowers a note from its plain letter name, such as ♯.
whyItMatters: When you see a sign next to a note name on a chart or a song sheet, it is an accidental. It tells you to play a neighbouring key instead of the plain white key.

meaning: One key lower. A flat sign (♭) after a note name means the key just to the left of that note.
whyItMatters: Many songs and band charts use flats: B♭, E♭ and A♭ come up all the time, especially with horn players. Knowing flats means you are never lost when someone calls one.

meaning: Two different names for the same key, such as C♯ and D♭.
whyItMatters: Both names are correct and you will hear both. Which one a song uses depends on its key, which comes in Unit 3. For now, if someone says D♭ and you think C♯, you are right.

meaning: A sign (♮) that cancels a sharp or flat and means the plain letter note.
whyItMatters: You will see ♮ on charts when a note should be the plain white key rather than its sharp or flat neighbour.

meaning: The Indian names for the notes: Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni.
whyItMatters: If you sing or hear songs in sargam, you can now connect those names straight to the keys.

meaning: The first note of sargam: the home note of the song. Sa moves to wherever the song's home note is.
whyItMatters: Because Sa moves, a tune keeps the same sargam names whatever key you play it in. Tell the app where Sa is and it names the rest.

meaning: The plain, unchanged form of a sargam note.
whyItMatters: Shuddha notes are the starting point. The next lesson shows how some of them move one key up or down.

meaning: A sargam note lowered by one key. Re, Ga, Dha and Ni can be komal.
whyItMatters: Many ragas and film songs use komal notes, and they are the sargam names for most black keys.

meaning: A sargam note raised by one key. Only Ma can be tivra.
whyItMatters: Tivra Ma gives some ragas their bright, lifted sound. With komal and tivra, every key on the keyboard has a sargam name.

meaning: The smallest distance on the keyboard: from one key to the very next key. Also called a semitone.
whyItMatters: The half step is the ruler of music: every distance between notes is measured by counting half steps. When a band mate says "take it up a half step", they want the whole song one key higher.

meaning: Two half steps: a move that skips over exactly one key. Also called a whole tone.
whyItMatters: Most tunes move mainly in half steps and whole steps. Telling the two apart is the first step to hearing how a tune is built.

meaning: The distance between two notes, counted in half steps and given a name.
whyItMatters: Bands talk in intervals: "go up a 5th", "the harmony sits a few notes above". Intervals are also what the notes a band plays together are built from, so they lead into everything after this unit.

meaning: Two notes at exactly the same pitch: an interval of zero half steps.
whyItMatters: When the band plays "in unison", everyone plays the same notes together. It is also where counting starts: 0 half steps.

meaning: An interval that spans two letter names, such as C to D or E to F.
whyItMatters: The number tells you how many letters the interval covers. That is how musicians describe tunes and name the notes they play together.

meaning: The smaller of the two sizes an interval can come in, such as a minor 2nd (1 half step).
whyItMatters: Minor intervals tend to give music a darker colour. You will hear the word "minor" about other things later in this course too.

meaning: The bigger of the two sizes an interval can come in, such as a major 2nd (2 half steps).
whyItMatters: Major intervals give music its brighter colour. "Major" and "minor" are two of the words your band uses most.

meaning: An interval of 1 half step.
whyItMatters: It is the tightest, most tense interval. Think of the Jaws theme.

meaning: An interval of 2 half steps: a whole step.
whyItMatters: It is the most common move in tunes. Happy Birthday steps up a major 2nd on "-py birth".

meaning: An interval that spans three letter names, such as C to E.
whyItMatters: The notes a band plays together are often stacked a 3rd apart. In Unit 4 you will build them from the 3rds in this lesson.

meaning: An interval of 3 half steps.
whyItMatters: The minor 3rd gives music its sad, dark colour. Greensleeves opens with one.

meaning: An interval of 4 half steps.
whyItMatters: The major 3rd gives music its bright, happy colour. Oh When the Saints opens with one.

meaning: The label for the unison, 4th, 5th and octave: intervals with one main size that sound open and stable.
whyItMatters: When someone says "a perfect 4th", the word perfect tells you it is the plain, stable version of that interval.

meaning: An interval of 5 half steps, such as C to F.
whyItMatters: It is the sound of Here Comes the Bride, and of many bass lines that jump around a song.

meaning: An interval of 7 half steps, such as C to G.
whyItMatters: It is the open sound of rock guitar, and a low note plus the note a 5th above is how many left hands start. Twinkle Twinkle jumps up a 5th on the second "twinkle".

meaning: An interval of 6 half steps: exactly half an octave.
whyItMatters: The tritone sounds tense, as if it wants to move. It is the tension that pulls a song back home, which you will hear more of in Unit 6.

meaning: An interval of 8 half steps, such as C to A♭.
whyItMatters: It has a bittersweet sound, and it turns up in a lot of film and love-song melodies.

meaning: An interval of 9 half steps, such as C to A.
whyItMatters: It sounds warm and sweet, and it is the sound of many harmony lines. My Bonnie Lies Over the Ocean opens with one.

meaning: An interval of 10 half steps, such as C to B♭.
whyItMatters: The minor 7th is the "7" in names like G7 on a band chart, which you will meet in Unit 6. The original Star Trek theme opens with one.

meaning: An interval of 11 half steps, such as C to B.
whyItMatters: It is a dreamy, soft sound, all over soul, jazz and pop ballads.

meaning: Going up: from a lower note to a higher one.
whyItMatters: "Up a 5th" from C lands on G. Knowing the direction tells you which key to aim for.

meaning: Going down: from a higher note to a lower one.
whyItMatters: "Down a 5th" from C lands on F, not G. The same interval in the other direction reaches a different note.

meaning: Practice at recognising intervals and other sounds by ear.
whyItMatters: You already play by ear. Ear training puts names on what you hear, so when the band says "it goes up a 6th" you will recognise it at once.

meaning: A set of notes in order, going up or down from one note to the same letter an octave away.
whyItMatters: Most tunes are built from the notes of one scale. When a band mate says "just stay in the scale", they mean these notes will all fit.

meaning: The scale with the step pattern whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half: the sound of do re mi fa so la ti do.
whyItMatters: Most pop, film and folk tunes use the major scale. Its sound is so familiar that you recognise it at once.

meaning: The pattern of whole and half steps that builds a scale. The major scale's formula is W W H W W W H.
whyItMatters: The formula works from any starting note. Learn it once and you can build a major scale on any of the twelve keys, white or black.

meaning: The major scale that starts on C: C D E F G A B C, all white keys.
whyItMatters: It is the only major scale with no black keys, so it is the easiest one to see, and every other scale is compared with it.

meaning: The first note of a scale: the home note, where a tune feels finished.
whyItMatters: Songs usually end on the tonic. When you play by ear, the note that feels like home is the tonic, and finding it is the first step to working out what a song is built on.

meaning: A note's position in its scale, counted from the tonic as 1 up to 7.
whyItMatters: Numbers work in any key. When your band says "start on the 3" or "go to the 5", they mean scale degrees, and you will use them all through Unit 5.

meaning: The scale a song is built from, named after its tonic. A song in G major uses the G major scale and feels at home on G.
whyItMatters: "What key is it in?" is the first question a band asks. The key tells you which notes will fit and which black keys you will use.

meaning: The sharps or flats of a key, written once at the start of a piece of music.
whyItMatters: The number of sharps or flats tells you the key at a glance. On a chart, two sharps means the notes of D major.

meaning: The order sharps are added to key signatures: F♯ C♯ G♯ D♯ A♯ E♯ B♯.
whyItMatters: If a key has three sharps, you know which three: F♯, C♯ and G♯. No guessing.

meaning: The order flats are added to key signatures: B♭ E♭ A♭ D♭ G♭ C♭ F♭, the order of sharps backwards.
whyItMatters: Band charts are full of flat keys, especially with horns. Knowing the order tells you exactly which black keys a flat key uses.

meaning: All twelve major keys in a ring, each a perfect 5th from the next. One direction adds a sharp at each step; the other adds a flat.
whyItMatters: It is a map of how keys relate. Keys next to each other share all but one note, which is why songs often move to a neighbouring key, and why so much of Unit 5 follows the circle.

meaning: A scale with a darker sound than the major scale, with a minor 3rd between its tonic and its 3rd degree.
whyItMatters: Sad songs, many film themes and lots of rock are in minor keys. Telling major from minor is one of the first things a band ear needs.

meaning: The basic minor scale, with the step pattern W H W W H W W. A natural minor is A B C D E F G A.
whyItMatters: There are other minor scales you may meet later, but the natural minor is the one the others start from, and the one most songs use.

meaning: The minor key that shares all its notes with a major key. It starts on the major key's 6th degree, 3 half steps below its tonic.
whyItMatters: Relative keys share a key signature, so one sharp could mean G major or E minor. Lots of songs move between the two.

meaning: The major key that shares all its notes with a minor key, 3 half steps above the minor tonic.
whyItMatters: If a song in a minor key brightens up halfway through, it has often moved to its relative major.

meaning: Three or more notes played at the same time.
whyItMatters: Chords are what the band plays under the tune. When someone says "the chords for this song", they mean these groups of notes, one after another.

meaning: A chord of three notes stacked in 3rds: a note, a 3rd above it, and a 3rd above that.
whyItMatters: Almost every chord on a band chart is a triad or is built from one. Learn the triad and you can play most songs.

meaning: The note a chord is built up from, and the note it is named after.
whyItMatters: When a band mate says "it's a G chord", G is the root. Bass players usually play the root, so it is the note your left hand will want.

meaning: A triad of a root, a major 3rd above it, and a perfect 5th above the root. It sounds bright.
whyItMatters: It is the most common chord in music. On a chart, a plain letter like "G" means a major triad.

meaning: One of the notes that make up a chord. A triad has three: the root, the 3rd and the 5th.
whyItMatters: Musicians name notes in a chord this way: "put the 3rd on top" means play E above the others in C major. A tune note that is a chord tone sounds settled over that chord.

meaning: A triad of a root, a minor 3rd above it, and a perfect 5th above the root. It sounds darker than major.
whyItMatters: Minor triads are the other half of most songs. Many pop songs use just four chords, and one or two of them are minor.

meaning: The short written name of a chord: its root, plus a tag for its kind. C means C major and Cm means C minor.
whyItMatters: This is how bands write songs down. A chart is a row of chord symbols over the lyrics, and you play each one as you reach it.

meaning: A triad of a root, a minor 3rd above it, and a tritone above the root. Written dim or °. It sounds tense.
whyItMatters: It is the only triad on the white keys that is neither major nor minor (B D F), and its tension pulls strongly to the next chord. You will see it often in Unit 5.

meaning: A triad of a root, a major 3rd above it, and a raised 5th (8 half steps) above the root. Written aug or +.
whyItMatters: It is rare, but it shows up as a dreamy, unsettled moment in ballads and old film music. If a chord sounds like it is floating, it may be augmented.

meaning: A chord with the 3rd replaced by a 2nd or a 4th. Written sus. It is neither major nor minor.
whyItMatters: Suspended chords add colour without the happy or sad label. They are all over pop and worship music, and guitarists love them.

meaning: A suspended chord with a major 2nd in place of the 3rd: root, 2nd, 5th. Csus2 is C D G.
whyItMatters: It has a bright, open sound. Swap a major chord for its sus2 and the song instantly sounds more modern.

meaning: A suspended chord with a perfect 4th in place of the 3rd: root, 4th, 5th. Csus4 is C F G.
whyItMatters: Sus4 to major is one of the most common moves in songs, often right at the end of a phrase. When you hear the chord "settle", that is often a sus4 resolving.

meaning: A chord built only from the notes of one key. In C major, every white-key triad is diatonic.
whyItMatters: Most songs use mostly diatonic chords. If you know a song is in G, you already know the seven chords it is most likely to use.

meaning: A number (I to VII) for a chord, from the scale degree of its root. Upper case is major, lower case is minor, ° is diminished.
whyItMatters: Numerals work in every key. "I–IV–V" is the same idea in C, in G or in E♭, so one pattern covers every song that uses it.

meaning: One of the three main chords of a key: I, IV and V. In C major, C, F and G.
whyItMatters: Thousands of songs use only these three chords. "Three chords and the truth" is a saying for a reason.

meaning: The 5th scale degree, and the V chord built on it. It pulls strongly back to the tonic.
whyItMatters: Songs build tension on V and release it on I. Hearing that pull lets you guess where a song is going next.

meaning: The 4th scale degree, and the IV chord built on it.
whyItMatters: When a band says "go to the four", they mean the subdominant. It is the usual first step away from I.

meaning: The minor chord on the 6th degree of a major key. In C major, A minor.
whyItMatters: It is the most common minor chord in pop. When a happy song turns wistful for a moment, it has often gone to the vi.

meaning: The minor chord on the 2nd degree of a major key. In C major, D minor.
whyItMatters: The ii often leads to V. It is a softer way to set up the pull back home, used all over jazz and soul.

meaning: The minor chord on the 3rd degree of a major key. In C major, E minor.
whyItMatters: It is the least used of the seven, so when a song does use it, it stands out as a fresh colour.

meaning: The diminished chord on the 7th degree of a major key. In C major, B diminished.
whyItMatters: It shares two notes with V and pulls hard to I, so it can stand in for V. You will meet it again in Unit 6.

meaning: Naming the chords of a key with plain numbers 1 to 7. A plain number means the chord the key itself gives on that degree.
whyItMatters: It is how most working bands call chords: "it's a 1-5-6-4 in G". Once you know the numbers, a chart works in any key the singer wants.

meaning: A series of chords played one after another, often written as numerals or numbers.
whyItMatters: A song is mostly a few progressions repeated: one for the verse, one for the chorus. Spot the progression and you can play along with the whole song.

meaning: The progression I, V, vi, IV (1-5-6-4). In C major, C G Am F.
whyItMatters: Let It Be, No Woman No Cry, With or Without You and hundreds more use it. Learn it in a few keys and you can join in on a lot of songs.

meaning: The progression ii, V, I (2-5-1). In C major, Dm G C.
whyItMatters: It is the most important progression in jazz, and it ends a lot of soul and pop phrases too. Hear it and you know home is coming.

meaning: A twelve-chord progression of I, IV and V: I I I I, IV IV I I, V IV I I.
whyItMatters: Blues, rock and roll and lots of funk are built on it. Band mates can jam on it with no rehearsal: someone just says "blues in G".

meaning: To move a song to a different key, keeping the same numerals or numbers.
whyItMatters: Singers ask for songs in the key that suits their voice. If you think in numbers, you can transpose on the spot.

meaning: A chord of four notes stacked in 3rds: root, 3rd, 5th and 7th.
whyItMatters: Jazz, soul, R&B and lots of pop use 7th chords instead of plain triads. They sound fuller and smoother.

meaning: A major 7th chord: a major triad plus a major 7th above the root. Cmaj7 is C E G B.
whyItMatters: It is the soft, dreamy sound of bossa nova, soul ballads and a lot of neo-soul. Swap I for Imaj7 and a song instantly sounds smoother.

meaning: A major triad plus a minor 7th above the root. Written with a plain 7: G7 is G B D F.
whyItMatters: It holds a tritone (B and F) that pulls hard to the tonic chord. V7 to I is the strongest "we're home" move there is, and the blues uses 7 chords everywhere.

meaning: A minor 7th chord: a minor triad plus a minor 7th above the root. Am7 is A C E G.
whyItMatters: It is the mellow minor sound of soul, funk and jazz. ii7–V7–I is the jazz turnaround with 7ths added.

meaning: A diminished triad plus a minor 7th above the root. Written m7♭5 or ø. Bm7♭5 is B D F A.
whyItMatters: It is the vii chord of a major key with its 7th, and the ii chord of a minor key. Minor-key jazz ballads lean on it for their ii–V–i.

meaning: A chord of three stacked minor 3rds. Written dim7 or °7. Bdim7 is B D F A♭.
whyItMatters: Every note is 3 half steps from the next, so it sounds suspended in mid-air. It is a classic passing chord between two others, and the spooky sound of old film scores.

meaning: A triad plus a major 6th above the root. C6 is C E G A; Am6 is A C E F♯.
whyItMatters: It is the sweet, swing-era sound of a final chord in old standards and Beatles songs. Pianists often use C6 in place of plain C.

meaning: The 2nd counted from the octave above: 14 half steps above the root. D is the 9th of C.
whyItMatters: Chord names past 7 (9, 11, 13) count this way. Knowing the 9th is the 2nd tells you which key to add.

meaning: A triad plus the 9th, with no 7th. Cadd9 is C E G D.
whyItMatters: It is the open, ringing sound of modern pop and worship music. Guitarists play Cadd9 more than plain C in many songs.

meaning: A chord note past the 7th: the 9th, the 11th or the 13th.
whyItMatters: Jazz and gospel players add extensions for colour. A chart that says C9 or G13 is asking for them.

meaning: A dominant 7th chord plus the 9th. C9 is C E G B♭ D.
whyItMatters: It is the funk chord: James Brown built whole songs on one 9 chord.

meaning: A dominant 7th chord with the 9th and 11th added, usually played without the 3rd.
whyItMatters: It is the open, gospel and fusion sound, a bit like a 7sus4 with extra colour.

meaning: A dominant 7th chord with the 13th (the 6th, an octave up). Usually played as root, 3rd, 7th and 13th.
whyItMatters: It is the rich, bluesy dominant chord of jazz and soul. Many players use G13 in place of G7.

meaning: A chord symbol with a slash, like C/E: the chord C with E as the lowest note.
whyItMatters: Slash chords make bass lines walk smoothly: C, C/B, Am, Am/G steps down one note at a time. Band charts are full of them.

meaning: A song written as its tune with chord symbols above it.
whyItMatters: It is the standard way bands share songs. Read the symbols and you can play along with any song on a lead sheet.

meaning: How a chord's notes are arranged on the keyboard: their order, their octaves, and how spread out they are.
whyItMatters: Band keyboard players rarely play every chord from its root. Choosing voicings is how they sound smooth and stay out of the bass player's and singer's way.

meaning: A chord laid out with its root as the lowest note.
whyItMatters: Root position sounds the most solid and settled. It is the layout to fall back on, and the one other layouts are named against.

meaning: A chord laid out with its 3rd as the lowest note. C major in first inversion is E G C.
whyItMatters: First inversion sounds lighter than root position, and it lets the bass climb or fall step by step. On a chart, C/E is C in first inversion.

meaning: A chord laid out with its 5th as the lowest note. C major in second inversion is G C E.
whyItMatters: Second inversion is the handiest layout for many changes: C in second inversion to F in root position moves only two fingers, by a step each.

meaning: A 7th chord laid out with its 7th as the lowest note. G7 in third inversion is F G B D.
whyItMatters: With the 7th in the bass, the chord wants to fall a half step to the next one: G7/F to C/E is a classic smooth bass line.

meaning: The lowest note of a chord as it is played.
whyItMatters: The bass note shapes how a chord feels more than any other note. In a band the bass player usually plays it, so keep your left hand from clashing with theirs.

meaning: Moving from one chord to the next so each note moves as little as possible.
whyItMatters: Good voice leading is why a band keyboard player sounds smooth instead of jumpy, and it keeps your hand in one place on the keyboard.

meaning: A note that two chords share.
whyItMatters: Holding common tones is the simplest voice-leading trick there is. It makes chord changes smooth with almost no effort.

meaning: A chord played with just its root, 3rd and 7th, leaving out the 5th.
whyItMatters: It is the classic left-hand shape for jazz and soul piano: light, clear, and it leaves the right hand free for the tune.
